title: The Earth Turned Upside Down
sum: Chapter 24 opens the section that scholars call the "Isaiah Apocalypse" (chapters 24–27). After eleven chapters of oracles against single nations (13–23), the scene widens to the whole earth. The LORD empties the world, its people and priests, its markets and parties, because they have broken "the everlasting covenant" (24:5). A curse eats the earth, the wine and music stop, the "city of chaos" falls, and only a few survivors are left, like olives after the harvest.

Distant voices start to sing (24:14–16), but the prophet cannot join them: betrayal is still at work, and no one escapes terror, trench and trap. The floodgates of heaven open as in Noah's day, the earth reels like a drunk, and the LORD judges the powers in heaven and the kings on earth. The chapter ends with the LORD reigning on Mount Zion, so bright that the sun and moon are ashamed.
readings: Read as world judgment

Most readers, Jewish and Christian, have read the chapter as the end of the present world: a judgment on all humanity and on the heavenly powers, followed by God's open reign. On this reading the flood imagery of 24:18, the cosmic shaking of 24:19–20 and the prison of 24:22 describe the last day, and Revelation's use of the same pictures shows how the early church heard them.
Read as Judah's history widened

Others stress the local details: a city, its gate, its wine, its priests and its debts. The prophet takes judgments he had seen or expected, Assyria's ravaging of the land and a city's fall, and paints them on a world-sized canvas. The "earth" is also the land of Judah, and the readers are meant to see their own ruin as part of God's dealings with the whole world.
Read as un-creation

The chapter can be read against Genesis 1–9. The earth returns to tohu (24:10, Genesis 1:2), the windows of the flood reopen (24:18), and Noah's everlasting covenant is broken (24:5). Sin undoes creation. The new creation of 25:6–8 and 26:19 then answers it.

views.H: Readers who look for a historical setting connect the chapter to a fallen city: Babylon in 689 BC, when Sennacherib flooded it, or in 539, when Cyrus took it; Samaria in 722; or Jerusalem in 587, with its priests and people carried off (24:2, 11). Traditional interpreters who hold that Isaiah wrote the chapter in the 700s BC read it as a prophetic picture of judgments still to come, of which Assyria's and Babylon's conquests were the first installments.
views.C: Most critical scholars think chapters 24–27 were written later than Isaiah of Jerusalem and placed here to round off the oracles against the nations. Dates proposed range from the 500s BC to the 300s (Millar, Johnson, Wildberger, Blenkinsopp). Bernhard Duhm (1892) dated them as late as the 100s BC, but the Greek translation of Isaiah, made in the 100s BC, and the Great Isaiah Scroll (about 125 BC) already contain them, so very late dates are now rare, though Otto Kaiser still argues for a Hellenistic date. Others go the other way and place the chapters in the 700s BC, tied to the Assyrian campaigns of the 720s (Hayes and Irvine). Scholars also note how much of the chapter reuses other Scripture: Genesis, Amos, Hosea and other parts of Isaiah (Hibbard, Polaski).
views.J: The Targum reads 24:23 as the revelation of the kingdom of the LORD of hosts on Mount Zion, and so joins it to the feast of 25:6. Rabbinic readers set the verse beside 30:26, where the moon shines like the sun, and solved the tension by assigning one verse to the days of the Messiah and the other to the world to come (Bavli Sanhedrin 91b).
views.X: Christian writers read the chapter of the last judgment. The shaking of earth and heaven, the darkening of sun and moon and the binding of powers in a pit all return in Revelation (6:12–17; 20:1–3), and the elders before God's glory reappear around the throne (Revelation 4:4). Jerome and medieval interpreters took the "city of chaos" as the world under sin, and the singers from the ends of the earth as the Gentiles who would believe the gospel.
views.F: Futurist readers see a still-coming judgment of the whole earth, followed by God's kingdom on earth. Many dispensational and premillennial interpreters link 24:21–23 with Revelation 20: the powers are shut in a pit, "after many days" they are dealt with again, and the LORD reigns from Jerusalem (Walvoord). Amillennial readers see the final judgment and the new creation, with no earthly interval.

deep.b:
Since the 1800s scholars have called chapters 24–27 the "Isaiah Apocalypse" because they share features with later Jewish apocalypses such as Daniel 7–12 and 1 Enoch: judgment on the whole world, cosmic signs in sun and moon, heavenly powers imprisoned, a feast on God's mountain, death swallowed up, the dead raised (26:19), the monster Leviathan slain (27:1) and a great trumpet calling the exiles home (27:13). Yet these chapters lack what defines an apocalypse in the strict sense: a seer who is shown visions and has them explained by an angel (see the topic page). Many scholars therefore call them "proto-apocalyptic": prophecy on its way to becoming apocalyptic (Hanson, Millar, Collins).

The section is also a set of songs. Laments over the earth (24:1–13, 16–20) alternate with hymns of the rescued (25:1–5; 26:1–6), and a prayer of waiting (26:7–19) is answered by promises "on that day" (27:1–13). Most scholars read the four chapters as one composition, though some think they grew over time around an older core.

In Isaiah's own day (the 700s BC). Conservative interpreters such as Edward J. Young, John Oswalt and Alec Motyer hold that Isaiah wrote these chapters as the climax of the oracles against the nations. They note that Isaiah's vocabulary appears throughout ("on that day," the remnant, the vineyard of chapter 5 sung again in 27:2–6), and that nothing requires a later date if a prophet could see beyond his own time. They also note that 24–27 draw on Isaiah's own earlier oracles.

After the exile (500s–300s BC). Most critical scholars place the chapters later. They point to the broad, world-wide outlook, the resurrection hope of 26:19, the angelic powers of 24:21 and the combat with Leviathan, all of which become common in later Jewish writings. Suggested settings include the late 500s BC, around Babylon's fall (Millar), the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall in 587 (Johnson), or the Persian period more broadly (Wildberger, Blenkinsopp). Duhm's date in the 100s BC is ruled out for most by the Greek translation and the Qumran scrolls, though Kaiser still argues for a Hellenistic date, and Hayes and Irvine place the chapters in the 700s BC, in the time of the Assyrian campaigns of the 720s.

A book read as a whole. Recent scholars, whatever their dating, stress that the chapters were placed after 13–23 on purpose: the nations judged one by one are now judged together, and Zion's future is set against the fall of the world's proud city (Childs, Sweeney, Seitz).

The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew of the Leningrad Codex. For every verse of chapters 24–30 the Dead Sea Scrolls were read directly in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription (through the site's tools): the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, complete), 1QIsa-b (1Q8), and the fragments 4QIsa-b, -c, -f and -k (4Q56, 4Q57, 4Q60, 4Q64). The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus; readings of Ziegler's critical text, of Theodotion and Aquila, and of the Targum are given as reported by Ziegler, Chilton and the commentaries named, unless a note says otherwise. The Targum was checked directly for 24:23, 25:6, 26:19, 27:1 and 28:16. Later Greek versions (Theodotion, Aquila), the Latin Vulgate and medieval Hebrew manuscripts were not read directly and are cited as reported in Ziegler, BHS and the commentaries.

echoes: Genesis 1:2; Genesis 7:11; Genesis 9:16; Exodus 24:9–11; Hosea 4:1–9; Amos 5:19; Jeremiah 48:43–44; Psalm 93:1; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6; Revelation 4:4; Revelation 6:12–17; Revelation 11:15; Revelation 20:1–3

settings.what: A lament over the emptied earth
settings.by: The prophet, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, who overhear a judgment on the whole world
settings.when: Undated. Traditional readers place it in Isaiah's ministry (about 740–700 BC); most critical scholars place it after the exile
settings.why: The poem tells its hearers that sin is not a private matter: broken laws and bloodshed pollute the earth itself, and no rank or wealth protects anyone. Hearing a world-wide judgment in the language of their own covenant, the people of Judah are meant to see their own guilt in the world's, and to stop trusting in the city and its festivals.
settings.readers: For readers of the finished book, 24 gathers up the oracles against the nations (13–23) into one final judgment, so that Babylon, Moab, Egypt and Tyre become pictures of one proud world.
views: A prophecy of Isaiah in the 700s BC about judgments to come (Young, Oswalt, Motyer).
A later poem from Isaiah's followers, written after a city's fall in the 500s–400s BC (Millar, Wildberger, Johnson).
A few critical scholars also date it to the 700s BC, in the time of the Assyrian campaigns of the 720s (Hayes and Irvine); Kaiser at the other end argues for a Hellenistic date.

settings.what: Songs from far away, and the prophet's reply
settings.by: Unnamed singers at the ends of the earth; then the prophet ("But I said")
settings.to: The LORD, praised by the singers; the prophet answers them, and the hearers listen in
settings.when: In the middle of the judgment, not after it
settings.why: The singers praise God too soon. The prophet's "I grow thin" warns his hearers not to celebrate while treachery is still at work. The scene teaches patience: praise is coming, but the reckoning must happen first.

settings.what: No escape, and the LORD's reign
settings.to: "You who live on the earth" (24:17), with Judah listening
settings.when: Undated
settings.why: The hearers are told that no one can outrun God's judgment, but also that it ends in the LORD reigning on Zion. The promise of 24:23 gives the people of Jerusalem a reason to hold on: their city will become the throne of the world's true King.
settings.readers: Later readers, Jewish and Christian, read these verses as the end of history and the start of God's kingdom (Revelation 4; 20).

traditions.q: The powers on high are locked in a pit and, "after many days," called to account (24:21–23), and then the LORD reigns from Zion. Does this describe a thousand-year reign of Christ on earth?
views: Yes. The prison of 24:22 is the abyss of Revelation 20:1–3, the "many days" are the thousand years, and the LORD's reign on Mount Zion is Christ's earthly kingdom in Jerusalem before the final judgment (Walvoord; Pentecost).

Divided. Many Baptists are premillennial, as above, and some historic premillennialists read the passage of Christ's return and reign (Ladd); others are amillennial. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) affirms Christ's personal, visible return without deciding the millennium.

No earthly interval is meant. The passage pictures the final judgment of all powers and God's eternal reign; Satan's binding in Revelation 20 is his restraint during the church age, and the reign is heavenly and then the new creation (Hoekema).
The Church rejects a future earthly messianic kingdom before the end (Catechism 676). The passage is read of Christ's victory, the last judgment and the glory of the heavenly Jerusalem.

The thousand years of Revelation 20 are spent by the saints in heaven while the earth lies empty and Satan is bound to it; the empty, shaken earth of Isaiah 24 is often read as a picture of that desolate earth (White, The Great Controversy).

No earthly kingdom of the saints comes before the resurrection. The Augsburg Confession (Article XVII) condemns those who teach that the godly will possess a worldly kingdom before the dead are raised; the reign is Christ's now and then forever.

The Church confesses that Christ's kingdom "will have no end," and Orthodox teachers have generally read the thousand years of Revelation 20 as the present age, not as a separate earthly reign; Isaiah's judgment and the LORD's reign on Zion look to the last day and the age to come (Ware).

title: Death Swallowed Up
sum: Chapter 25 answers the gloom of chapter 24 with song. A voice thanks God for bringing down the fortified city of outsiders and for being a fortress to the poor (25:1–5). Then comes one of the great promises of the Bible: on Mount Zion the LORD of Armies will spread a feast of the richest food and finest wine for all the peoples, tear away the veil of grief that covers the nations, swallow up death forever and wipe the tears from every face (25:6–8).

The rescued respond, "Here he is, our God! We hoped in him, that he would rescue us" (25:9). The chapter closes on a harsh note: Moab, the proud neighbor, is trodden down like straw in a manure pit (25:10–12). The feast for all nations and the fall of the proud belong together.
readings: Read as the end of death

Most Jewish and Christian readers have heard 25:8 as the end of death itself. The Mishnah closes its laws of mourning with it, Paul ends his defense of the resurrection with it (1 Corinthians 15:54), and Revelation uses its promise of wiped tears for the new creation (Revelation 21:4). On this reading the feast is the banquet of the age to come.
Read as national restoration

Others read the language as a poetic picture of rescue in history: "death" is exile, oppression and defeat, and its swallowing is Israel's restoration, as in Ezekiel's valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37). The feast celebrates God's kingship on Zion, as royal enthronements were celebrated with meals (1 Kings 1:25; 1 Samuel 11:15).
Read as a feast of judgment

The Targum turns the feast into a cup of judgment for the nations: they expect glory and receive plagues. The picture of a sacrificial feast for God's enemies appears elsewhere (34:6; Jeremiah 46:10; Zephaniah 1:7; Revelation 19:17–18).

views.H: Readers who look for a historical event behind 25:1–5 connect the fallen city with Babylon (689 or 539 BC), Samaria, or a Moabite capital. The feast on Zion is then the coronation meal of God's kingship (24:23), when the nations who had come to plunder Jerusalem come instead to worship.
views.C: Critical scholars see 25:6–8 as one of the latest and boldest texts of the Hebrew Bible, a step toward the resurrection hope of 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. Some think 25:8a ("He will swallow death") was added to the feast scene later. The language of Death swallowed probably draws on Canaanite mythology of the god Mot (Day, Smith).
views.J: Rabbinic tradition cites 25:8 for the world to come: Mishnah Moed Katan 3:9 ends its laws of mourning with it, and the Talmud sets it against 65:20, where people still die, by assigning one verse to Israel and the other to the nations (Bavli Pesachim 68a). The banquet of the righteous, with Leviathan's flesh, appears in Bavli Bava Batra 74b–75a. The Targum makes the feast a judgment on the nations.
views.X: The New Testament takes up the verse for the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:54) and the new creation (Revelation 7:17; 21:4). Jesus' sayings about the feast in the kingdom (Matthew 8:11; Luke 14:15–24) and the Last Supper's "until that day, the day I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father" (Matthew 26:29) have led many churches to read the Lord's Supper as a foretaste of this banquet. Christian art and liturgy use 25:6–9 at funerals and at Easter.
views.F: Futurist readers place the feast at Christ's return: for many premillennial interpreters it is the inauguration of his reign on Mount Zion, and for others the eternal state after the last enemy, death, is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26). Jewish hope places it in the days of the Messiah and the world to come.

deep.b:
The Hebrew of 25:8 is short: billa' hammavet lanetsach, "he has swallowed death forever." The verb is a "prophetic perfect," a past tense used for a future so certain it is spoken as done. The old Greek translator read it with death as the subject: "Death, having prevailed, swallowed (them)." Later Jewish revisers of the Greek corrected this. Theodotion's version, as reported in the critical apparatus, reads "Death was swallowed up in victory," which is word for word what Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:54. Paul then adds a line from Hosea 13:14 in his own Greek wording: "Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?"

Paul's "in victory" (eis nikos) comes from the double sense of netsach. In biblical Hebrew lanetsach usually means "forever," but in Aramaic and later Hebrew the root means "to win." Both senses make good theology: God's swallowing of death is permanent, and it is a victory. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew meaning, "for all time."

deep.h: The banquet in Jewish and Christian hope
deep.b:
Royal coronations and covenant-makings were sealed with meals (Exodus 24:11; 1 Samuel 11:15; 1 Kings 1:25). Isaiah's feast follows the LORD's enthronement on Zion (24:23), so it is a coronation banquet, but the guests are "all the peoples." Later Jewish writings develop the theme: 1 Enoch 62:14 has the righteous eat with the Son of Man; 2 Baruch 29:4–8 and 4 Ezra 6:49–52 keep Behemoth and Leviathan as food for the last days; the Talmud tells of a feast for the righteous made from Leviathan (Bavli Bava Batra 74b–75a). The Qumran Rule of the Congregation (1QSa II) pictures a meal at which the Messiah of Israel is present.

In the Gospels, Jesus' meals with outsiders and his parable of the great banquet (Luke 14:15–24) draw on the same hope, and the Last Supper looks ahead to the day Jesus will drink the cup "new with you in the kingdom of my Father" (Matthew 26:29). Revelation calls it "the wedding supper of the Lamb" (Revelation 19:9). Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant liturgies speak of the Eucharist or Lord's Supper as a foretaste of the heavenly banquet.
deep.refs: 25:6–9; Exodus 24:11; Matthew 8:11; Matthew 26:29; Luke 14:15–24; Revelation 19:9; 1 Enoch 62:14; 2 Baruch 29:4–8; 4 Ezra 6:49–52; 1QSa II, 11–22

echoes: Exodus 24:9–11; Hosea 13:14; Psalm 9:9; Matthew 8:11; Matthew 26:29; Luke 14:15–24; 1 Corinthians 15:54–55; Revelation 7:17; Revelation 19:9; Revelation 21:4; Jeremiah 48:1–47

settings.what: A song of thanks for a fallen city
settings.by: An individual singer ("my God"), speaking for the rescued
settings.to: The LORD, with the community listening
settings.when: After an oppressive city has fallen; the city is not named
settings.why: The song teaches the poor and powerless that God is on their side: the city that crushed them is gone, and even brutal nations end up honoring God. It gives the hearers words to praise God for history's reversals.
settings.readers: Readers of the finished book could hear Babylon, Nineveh or any oppressor in the nameless city.
views: The fallen city is an enemy stronghold of the 700s BC, and the singer a believer in Hezekiah's time.
The city is Babylon or another conqueror's town, and the song is the thanks of the restored community.

settings.what: The promise of the feast on Mount Zion
settings.to: Judah, about "all the peoples"
settings.when: Spoken of a future day ("on that day," 25:9), after the LORD begins to reign on Zion (24:23)
settings.why: The promise lifts the hearers' eyes beyond Judah's suffering to a day when God feeds the nations, ends grief and destroys death itself. It tells a small, often humiliated people that their God will one day be host to the whole world.
settings.readers: Later Jewish readers heard the age to come; Christians heard the resurrection and the kingdom banquet.

settings.what: A word against Moab
settings.to: Judah, about Moab
settings.when: Undated
settings.why: The joy of the feast does not cancel justice: pride that sets itself against God is brought down. For Judah's hearers, Moab's humiliation answered years of hostility and mockery.

title: Your Dead Will Live
sum: Chapter 26 is a song and a prayer. It opens with a hymn that Judah will sing "on that day" about its strong city, whose walls are God's rescue, and about the proud town brought low under the feet of the poor (26:1–6). Then the singers wait for God in the night, confess that other masters have ruled them, and lament that all their labor has given birth only to wind (26:7–18).

Into that lament comes one of the boldest lines in the Hebrew Bible: "Your dead will live! My corpses will rise!" (26:19). The dust-dwellers are called to wake and sing, and the earth gives birth to its dead. The chapter ends with God's people told to shut themselves in, like Israel on Passover night, while the LORD comes out to judge the earth, which will lay bare the blood it has hidden (26:20–21).
readings: Read as resurrection

Most Jewish and Christian readers have heard 26:19 as a promise that the dead will rise bodily. The Talmud cites it as proof of the resurrection, the Targum reads it of God reviving the dead, and Christian readers see it fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and the general resurrection at his return.
Read as national revival

Some scholars read 26:19 like Ezekiel 37: Israel, crushed and nearly dead as a nation, will live again. The contrast with 26:14 (the oppressor nations will not rise) and the labor imagery of 26:17–18 (the nation cannot bring itself to birth) support this collective reading.
Read as a liturgy

Others read the chapter as a liturgy for worship: a hymn (26:1–6), a community lament (26:7–18), an oracle of salvation in answer (26:19), and a word of instruction (26:20–21). On this reading the voices change, and 26:19 is God's or the prophet's answer to the people's despair.

views.H: Readers looking for a historical setting place the chapter in the return from exile or the Persian period, when Judah was small ("you have added to the nation," 26:15) and had been ruled by foreign masters (26:13). Older conservative readers place it in Hezekiah's day, after Assyria's defeat.
views.C: Critical scholars see 26:19 as a key witness to the rise of resurrection belief in Israel, older than Daniel 12:2 (about 165 BC) but later than most of the prophets. Some date the verse late, in the Hellenistic era, as an addition to an earlier lament; others see it as an original part of the chapter that drew on older images of God as the one who gives life (1 Samuel 2:6; Hosea 6:2).
views.J: The Talmud treats 26:19 as proof that resurrection is taught in the Prophets (Bavli Sanhedrin 90b), and the Targum says, "You are he who brings the dead to life." Rabbinic tradition speaks of the "dew of resurrection" stored in heaven (Bavli Chagigah 12b), and the Amidah joins the falling dew with the blessing "who gives life to the dead." Rabbi Elazar taught that "dew of lights" is the light of Torah, which revives those who follow it (Bavli Ketubot 111b).
views.X: Christian writers from the second century on cite 26:19 for the resurrection of the body, often beside Daniel 12:2 and Ezekiel 37. The opening of tombs at Jesus' death (Matthew 27:52–53) and Jesus' word "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25) are read as the beginning of what Isaiah promised. Some read "my corpse" (26:19) as Christ speaking, with his people rising in him.
views.F: Futurist readers place 26:19 at the resurrection when Christ returns. Many premillennial interpreters see it as the resurrection of Old Testament believers at his coming after the tribulation, followed by the hiding of 26:20 and the judgment of 26:21.

deep.h: Resurrection in the Hebrew Bible: where 26:19 stands
deep.b:
Most of the Hebrew Bible speaks of the dead going down to Sheol, a shadowy place from which no one returns. Job asks, "When a man dies, can he come back to life?" (Job 14:14), and a psalmist asks whether the shades will "get up and give you thanks" (Psalm 88:10). Yet there are early hints that God's power reaches even there: "The LORD kills and makes alive; he takes down to Sheol, and he brings up" (1 Samuel 2:6). Hosea speaks of the nation raised "on the third day" (Hosea 6:2), and Ezekiel sees dry bones rise as a sign of Israel's return (Ezekiel 37).

Isaiah 26:19 goes further. It is set against 26:14, where the dead oppressors will not rise, and it uses bodily words: "corpses," "dust," and the same verb "rise" that is denied to the dead oppressors in 26:14. Daniel 12:2 seems to draw on it, since both speak of those who "lie" or "sleep" in the dust waking up. By the time of 2 Maccabees 7 and the Pharisees, resurrection was a central hope, and the rabbis and the early church both cited this verse for it. Jon Levenson argues that resurrection grew from Israel's older belief in God's power to restore his people, so the "national" and "personal" readings belong to one hope.
deep.refs: 26:14; 26:19; Job 14:14; Psalm 88:10; 1 Samuel 2:6; Hosea 6:2; Ezekiel 37:1–14; Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7:9

echoes: Psalm 118:19–20; Psalm 24:7; Psalm 63:1–6; Genesis 4:10; Genesis 7:16; Exodus 12:22–23; Ezekiel 37:1–14; Daniel 12:2; Matthew 6:6; Matthew 27:52–53; John 11:25; John 16:21; Philippians 2:13; Revelation 6:9–10

settings.what: The song of the strong city
settings.by: The people of Judah, as the prophet gives them the words
settings.to: God, and one another, in worship
settings.when: "On that day," after the proud city has fallen
settings.why: The song gives a weak, threatened people the words of the victory they do not yet see. It teaches them that their safety lies in God's rescue rather than in walls, and that the proud will be trodden down by the poor.
views: Judah sings of a strong city while Assyria threatens, and promises that the proud will fall.
The small restored community of Jerusalem, rebuilt but weak under foreign rulers, sings the song.

settings.what: A prayer of the community in the night
settings.by: The community of the faithful, speaking as "we" and "I"
settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: A time of distress and foreign domination, while they wait for God's judgment to come
settings.why: The prayer gives voice to longing, confession and honest despair. It admits that the people cannot save themselves (26:18) and so prepares them to hear the promise that only God can bring life out of death.
views: Many scholars hear the prayer of a small community under foreign masters after the exile.
Some conservative scholars connect it with Judah's distress under Assyria in the 700s BC.

settings.what: The promise that the dead will live
settings.by: The prophet, or God speaking through him ("my corpses")
settings.to: The praying community
settings.when: In answer to the lament of 26:7–18
settings.why: The promise answers despair with resurrection: what the people could not bring to birth, God will. For a community that had seen its people die under oppression, it said that their dead were not lost.
views: "Your dead" and "my corpses" are both God's words: the dead belong to him.
The prophet answers the people and claims the dead as his own people.

settings.what: A call to hide while the LORD judges
settings.by: The prophet, speaking for God ("my people")
settings.to: God's people, in the same situation as 26:7–18 (see the date views there)
settings.when: As the LORD comes out to judge the earth
settings.why: The call reassures the faithful that judgment will pass over them, as on Passover night, and that hidden violence will at last be brought to light.

traditions.q: Isaiah 26:19 promises that "your dead will live." Will all the dead rise together at the end, or in stages?
views: There is one resurrection of all the dead, "both the just and the unjust," on the last day, when Christ returns; souls already enjoy or lack the sight of God before that day (Catechism 997–1001, 1038).

At the last day all the dead will be raised with the same bodies, the unjust to dishonor and the just to honor, in one general resurrection followed by the last judgment (Westminster Confession 32.2–3).

In stages: the church is raised at the rapture, and Old Testament believers, the subject of Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2, are raised at Christ's return after the tribulation; the wicked are raised after the thousand years (Pentecost, Things to Come).
The dead are unconscious until they are raised. The righteous rise at Christ's second coming; the wicked rise at the end of the thousand years for final judgment (Fundamental Beliefs 26–27).

A small number (the 144,000) are raised to heavenly life; most of the dead, both righteous and unrighteous, will be raised to life on a renewed earth during Christ's thousand-year reign (Insight on the Scriptures, "Resurrection").

Historic premillennialists, a large evangelical stream, hold two stages around the thousand years: the righteous are raised when Christ returns, before the thousand years, and the rest of the dead after them, following Revelation 20:4–6. This differs from the dispensational scheme, which separates the church's rapture from the raising of Old Testament believers (Ladd). Amillennial evangelicals hold one general resurrection.
One general resurrection on the last day: Christ will come to judge and raise all the dead, and the godly go to eternal life, the ungodly to eternal punishment (Augsburg Confession, Article XVII).

One general resurrection of the dead at Christ's coming, confessed in the Creed ("I look for the resurrection of the dead"). Easter is its pledge, since Christ's rising has already opened the way (Ware).

title: Leviathan and the Vineyard
sum: Chapter 27 closes the "Isaiah Apocalypse" with four short pieces. First, the LORD takes his great sword to Leviathan, the fleeing and twisting serpent, the dragon of the sea, using the very names that Canaanite poets gave to the monster of chaos (27:1). Then comes a new vineyard song, which reverses the bitter song of 5:1–7: God now guards and waters his vineyard, has no anger left, and offers even its enemies peace (27:2–6).

Next, a meditation on Jacob's punishment: God struck Israel, but in measure, and its guilt will be atoned for when it smashes its altars to other gods, while a fortified city lies deserted (27:7–11). Last, the LORD beats out his harvest from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, gathers Israel one by one, and a great shofar calls the lost home from Assyria and Egypt to worship in Jerusalem (27:12–13).
readings: Read as the defeat of evil

Many readers take 27:1 as the climax of the Isaiah Apocalypse: God's final victory over every power of chaos and evil. Christian readers see it as the defeat of Satan, "that ancient serpent" (Revelation 12:9; 20:2), and the vineyard and the shofar as the restoration that follows.
Read as history in mythic dress

Others read the dragon as a code for empires, as the Targum and Rashi do. On this reading the chapter promises the fall of Israel's oppressors (Assyria, Egypt, Babylon or their successors) and the return of the scattered tribes.
Read as an anthology

Critical scholars often treat 27:1, 27:2–6, 27:7–11 and 27:12–13 as separate pieces placed together to close chapters 24–27. The order, from the defeat of the monster to the gathering of the exiles, gives the section a shape: judgment, restored people, worship on Zion.

views.H: Readers looking for history connect the three serpents with three empires (often Assyria, Babylon and Egypt, or Assyria, Egypt and Tyre), and the walled city of 27:10 with Samaria (722 BC), Babylon, or a Moabite city. The gathering from Assyria and Egypt fits the scattering of both northern Israel and Judah.
views.C: Critical scholars see in 27:1 one of the clearest cases of Canaanite myth in the Bible: the epithets match the Ugaritic texts word for word. Many date 27:7–11 to the Persian period and debate whether its deserted city is Jerusalem or a foreign capital. The vineyard song is widely read as a deliberate rewriting of 5:1–7.
views.J: The Targum turns the monsters into kings like Pharaoh and Sennacherib, and Rashi follows the Targum. The Talmud's tales of Leviathan being kept for the feast of the righteous (Bavli Bava Batra 74b–75a) draw on this verse. The "great shofar" of 27:13 is prayed for daily in the Amidah and read on Rosh Hashanah.
views.X: Christian readers have long read 27:1 of Christ's victory over Satan, with Revelation 12–13 and 20 as the key. Paul uses the Greek of 27:9, joined to 59:20–21, for the salvation of "all Israel" (Romans 11:26–27). The great trumpet of 27:13 is heard in Matthew 24:31 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16.
views.F: Futurist readers place 27:1 at Christ's return, with the binding of Satan (Revelation 20:2), and 27:12–13 at the final regathering of Israel to the land. Some Dispensationalists see the regathering beginning in modern Jewish return to the land.

deep.b:
The match between 27:1 and the Ugaritic Baal texts is exact enough that nearly all scholars accept a link: Litan (ltn), "the fleeing serpent" (btn brh), "the twisting serpent" (btn 'qltn) and the dragon (tnn) appear in KTU 1.5 i 1–3 and KTU 1.3 iii 38–42, tablets written down centuries before Isaiah. The same language appears in Job 3:8, Job 26:13, Psalm 74:13–14 and Isaiah 51:9. Israel's poets knew this imagery and used it.

What the borrowing means is debated. John Day argues that Israel took over the myth of a divine battle with the sea monster and applied it to the LORD's victories at creation, at the Exodus, and at the end. David Tsumura argues that the Bible uses the language poetically without accepting a real cosmic battle at creation; Genesis 1:21 makes the "great sea monsters" (tanninim) simple creatures. Both agree that Isaiah 27:1 moves the battle to the future: "on that day." The point is not a story about the gods, but a promise that whatever is hostile to God, in heaven or on earth, will be judged.
deep.refs: 27:1; 51:9–10; Job 3:8; Job 26:12–13; Job 41:1; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 104:26; Genesis 1:21; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2

echoes: Job 26:13; Job 41:1; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 80:8–16; Genesis 15:18; Ruth 2:17; Judges 12:6; Deuteronomy 24:1; Romans 11:26–27; Matthew 24:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16; John 15:1–8; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2

settings.what: The judgment of Leviathan
settings.to: God's people
settings.when: "On that day," a day of God's judgment: in history if Leviathan is an empire, or the end of history if Leviathan is the power of evil
settings.why: Using the most frightening images their world knew, the oracle tells the hearers that every power of chaos, whether empire or evil itself, will meet God's sword. It answers fear of the forces that seemed to rule history.
views: Leviathan is Assyria, Babylon, Egypt or a later power, as the Targum and Rashi read it.
Leviathan is the last power of evil, destroyed on the day of final judgment, as many Christian readers hear it (Oswalt).

settings.what: The new song of the vineyard
settings.by: The LORD, introduced by the prophet
settings.to: His people, the vineyard
settings.when: "On that day"; written as an answer to the song of 5:1–7
settings.why: For hearers who knew the earlier song of a vineyard abandoned, this song says the judgment is not God's last word: he will guard his people, hold no more anger, and even offer peace to their enemies.

settings.what: A meditation on Jacob's punishment and forgiveness
settings.to: Jacob (Israel)
settings.when: After a time of judgment and exile
settings.why: The words explain suffering as measured discipline rather than destruction and call the people to show their repentance by destroying their idols.
views: Many scholars hear a call to Judah after 587 BC, with the deserted city as Jerusalem or Samaria.
Others read the deserted city as the enemy capital, so the passage contrasts Israel's measured punishment with its enemy's ruin.

settings.what: The gathering of the scattered
settings.to: The people of Israel, many of them scattered
settings.when: "On that day"
settings.why: The promise tells scattered Israelites, in Assyria and Egypt and everywhere between, that not one of them is forgotten: God will gather them one by one and bring them to worship in Jerusalem.
views: The scattered are Israelites already carried off to Assyria or fled to Egypt after 722 BC.
The scattered are Jews living across the Persian world and Egypt.

title: A Covenant with Death
sum: Chapter 28 opens the "book of woes" (chapters 28–33). The first woe falls on Samaria, the proud capital of the northern kingdom, whose drunken leaders wear a fading crown; Assyria will swallow it like an early fig (28:1–6). Then the prophet turns on Jerusalem. Its priests and prophets reel from wine and mock Isaiah's message as baby talk, so God will speak to them in the foreign speech of invaders (28:7–13).

The rulers of Jerusalem boast of a "covenant with death" that will keep them safe from the flood, probably their treaty with Egypt. God answers by laying in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone: "Whoever believes will not hurry" (28:16). The shelter of lies will be swept away, and God will do his "strange" work against his own city (28:14–22). A parable of a farmer, who plows, plants and threshes each crop in the right way, closes the chapter: God's counsel is wonderful, and his judgment has a purpose (28:23–29).
readings: Read as politics

The chapter can be read as a commentary on Judah's foreign policy around 705–701 BC: the rulers trusted an alliance with Egypt against Assyria, and Isaiah called it a covenant with death. On this reading the cornerstone is God's promise to Zion, and "believing" means not panicking into treaties.
Read as messianic prophecy

The New Testament and much of Christian tradition read the cornerstone of 28:16 as Christ, the stone that is a foundation for those who trust and a stumbling stone for those who do not (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6–8). Jewish tradition, through the Targum, read it as a king appointed in Zion.
Read as wisdom

The farmer's parable invites a wisdom reading of the whole chapter: God's ways may seem strange (28:21), but like a farmer's seasons they are measured and fruitful. The mockers' "wisdom" (28:9–10, 28:15) is folly, and true wisdom begins with trust.

views.H: The oracle on Samaria comes from before 722 BC, and the oracles on Jerusalem from Hezekiah's revolt and alliance with Egypt (705–701 BC), when Sennacherib's army swept through Judah like a flood (2 Kings 18:13). The "strange work" is God's use of Assyria against Jerusalem; the cornerstone is his commitment to Zion, which held when Jerusalem survived in 701 BC.
views.C: Most critical scholars accept 28:1–4, 28:7–22 as largely from Isaiah of Jerusalem, with 28:5–6 as a later addition that turns the woe into a promise for the remnant. The farmer's parable (28:23–29) may be Isaiah's own or a later wisdom addition. The "covenant with death" is widely read as Isaiah's satire on the Egyptian treaty, possibly with a sideways glance at Canaanite and Egyptian cults of the dead.
views.J: The Targum turns the foundation stone into a king: "I am appointing a king in Zion." Jewish interpreters have read the drunken priests and prophets as a warning to religious leaders, and the farmer's parable as a lesson in God's measured judgment, which never destroys Israel completely.
views.X: For Christians the chapter's center is 28:16, quoted in Romans 9:33, Romans 10:11 and 1 Peter 2:6 and echoed in Ephesians 2:20 of Christ the cornerstone. Paul uses 28:11–12 in 1 Corinthians 14:21 for speaking in tongues as a sign to unbelievers. Luther's distinction between God's "alien" and "proper" work comes from 28:21.
views.F: Some futurist interpreters read the "covenant with death" as a picture of the covenant that a future world ruler makes with Israel (Daniel 9:27), which Isaiah's "an end, a settled end" (28:22) also echoes. Most read the cornerstone as already laid in Christ, with its full effect at his return.

deep.h: The cornerstone: from Isaiah to Qumran and the New Testament
deep.b:
Isaiah 28:16 is set against the rulers' false shelter (28:15). God himself lays a stone in Zion: tested, precious, a cornerstone, firmly founded. Some scholars take the last words, "Whoever believes will not hurry," as the stone's inscription. In Isaiah's day the stone was probably God's promise to Zion and to David's house, which called for trust rather than frantic diplomacy (7:9; 30:15).

Later readers made the stone a person or a community. The Targum reads "a king," and the Qumran Community Rule calls the council of the community "the tested wall, the precious cornerstone" (1QS VIII, 7–8), applying the verse to itself. The early Christians gathered several stone texts: Isaiah 8:14 (the stone people trip over), Isaiah 28:16 (the foundation stone) and Psalm 118:22 (the rejected stone that became the head of the corner). Paul merges 28:16 and 8:14 in Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6–8 lines up all three. In both the stone divides people: it is a foundation for those who trust and a stumbling block for those who refuse.
deep.refs: 28:16; 8:14–15; Psalm 118:22; Romans 9:32–33; Romans 10:11; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Matthew 21:42

deep.b:
Isaiah 28:9–13 is a rare glimpse of how a prophet's opponents answered him. The leaders, drunk at their feasts, ridicule Isaiah's message as fit only for weaned infants, a babble of tsav la-tsav, qav la-qav. Whether these are baby sounds, alphabet drill or real words ("command on command, line on line"), the effect is clear: his preaching is called repetitive and childish.

God's answer is to turn the mockery around. If they will not listen to plain words, they will hear God in the "jabbering lips and a strange tongue" of the Assyrian army, and his word will become for them the very nonsense they mocked. Paul took this verse in another direction, as a sign that tongues do not by themselves bring unbelievers to faith (1 Corinthians 14:21–25).

echoes: 8:14–15; 10:22–23; 2 Samuel 5:20; 1 Chronicles 14:16; Joshua 10:11; Deuteronomy 28:49; Deuteronomy 12:9; Psalm 118:22; Romans 9:33; Romans 10:11; 1 Corinthians 14:21; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Peter 2:6–8; Matthew 11:28; Matthew 21:42

settings.what: Woe to Samaria's drunkards
settings.to: Ephraim's drunkards, the ruling class of Samaria, who are addressed directly; Jerusalem overhears
settings.when: Before Assyria took Samaria in 722 BC
settings.why: The oracle exposes the pride and self-indulgence of Samaria's rulers and announces their sudden fall. For the Jerusalem audience it was a warning by example, and the added promise (28:5–6) tells the remnant that God himself will be their crown.
views: Some think Isaiah spoke it in the 720s, when Samaria's fall was near.
Many think it was placed here, or reused, to introduce the warnings to Jerusalem that follow (28:7, "these too").

settings.what: The drunken priests and prophets
settings.to: The priests and prophets of Jerusalem
settings.when: During a feast, perhaps in the years before 701 BC
settings.why: Isaiah answers the leaders' mockery of his message by turning their words back on them: they will hear God's word as foreign gibberish when the invaders come. The passage shows that the rejection of the message was itself becoming the judgment.

settings.what: The covenant with death and the stone in Zion
settings.by: Isaiah, speaking the word of the LORD
settings.to: "You men of mockery, you rulers of this people here in Jerusalem" (28:14): Hezekiah's officials
settings.when: Probably 705–701 BC, when Judah made a treaty with Egypt against Assyria
settings.why: The oracle tells Judah's policy-makers that the alliance they trust is a deal with death and will be swept away, and that the only secure foundation is the one God has laid in Zion, which calls for trust instead of panic.

settings.what: The farmer's parable
settings.by: Isaiah, speaking as a teacher of wisdom
settings.to: His hearers in Jerusalem
settings.when: Following the oracle of judgment
settings.why: The parable helps the hearers make sense of a frightening message. God's work, like a farmer's, has times and measures: plowing does not go on forever, and threshing does not crush the grain to dust. Judgment serves the harvest.

traditions.q: Paul quotes 28:11–12 when he discusses speaking in tongues (1 Corinthians 14:21). Do the gift of tongues and the other miraculous gifts continue in the church today?
views: Yes. Baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion, and its initial physical sign is speaking in tongues, as at Pentecost (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths 7–8).

Many Reformed teachers hold that the miraculous gifts were signs confirming the apostles and ceased with them (B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles); a growing number of Reformed Christians are open to their continuing. A second argument draws on this very text: Paul quotes 28:11 to make tongues a sign of judgment on unbelieving Israel, a sign that ended when that judgment fell in AD 70 (Robertson; Gaffin).

The Spirit's charisms, extraordinary or simple, are graces for building up the Church, to be received with gratitude and tested by the Church's pastors (Catechism 799–801); tongues are practiced in the Catholic Charismatic Renewal.

Divided. Many Baptists hold that the sign gifts have ceased or should be treated with great caution; others accept that they continue. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) speaks of the Spirit's gifts without settling the question.

The Spirit works through the Word and the sacraments (Augsburg Confession, Article V), and the confessions do not make tongues a sign of faith or of the Spirit. Many Lutheran churches treat the extraordinary gifts as not to be expected as the normal life of the church; Lutheran charismatics accept them.

The Spirit's gifts have never left the Church, but Orthodox spirituality puts holiness and discernment above any outward sign, and tongues as the expected proof of the Spirit is not an Orthodox teaching (Ware).

title: Ariel and the Sealed Scroll
sum: Chapter 29 begins with a woe on "Ariel," a code name for Jerusalem that means "altar hearth." God himself will besiege the city of David until its voice is a ghostly whisper from the dust. Then, suddenly, the attacking nations are blown away like chaff, and their hopes vanish like a hungry man's dream (29:1–8). But the people cannot see what God is doing. They are drunk without wine, their prophets asleep, and the whole vision is like a sealed scroll (29:9–12).

Their worship is lip service, "a command made by humans and learned by heart" (29:13), so God will confound their wise men. A third woe falls on those who hide their plans from God, as if the clay could tell the potter he understands nothing (29:15–16). The chapter ends in hope: the deaf will hear the scroll, the blind will see, the lowly will rejoice, the ruthless will vanish, and Jacob's children will hallow God's name (29:17–24).
readings: Read as the crisis of 701 BC

Most readers set the chapter in the Assyrian crisis: Jerusalem besieged by Sennacherib, brought to the brink, and then suddenly delivered (29:5–8; compare 37:36). The blindness and lip service of 29:9–14 describe Judah's leaders, and the hidden plans of 29:15 are the Egyptian alliance.
Read as a pattern of judgment and grace

Others read the chapter as a pattern seen throughout the book: God brings his people low, then rescues them, and turns blindness into sight. The movement from the sealed scroll (29:11) to the deaf who hear the scroll (29:18) shapes the whole chapter.
Read through the New Testament

Christian readers hear Jesus' words against hypocrisy (Matthew 15:8–9), Paul's argument about the wisdom of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:19) and about Israel's hardening (Romans 11:8), and Jesus' healings as the signs of 29:18 (Matthew 11:5).

views.H: The siege of Ariel is usually linked with Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC, when Jerusalem was surrounded and then spared (2 Kings 18–19; 37:36). The secret plans of 29:15 are the negotiations with Egypt (30:1–7). Some older readers also saw Jerusalem's later sieges by Babylon (587 BC) and Rome (AD 70) as fulfillments.
views.C: Critical scholars often distinguish Isaiah's original threat against Jerusalem (29:1–4, 29:9–10, 29:13–16) from later additions that turn it into hope (29:5–8, 29:17–24), though many now read the reversal as part of Isaiah's own message. The phrases "the prophets" and "the visionaries" in 29:10 are often taken as early scribal glosses.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads "Ariel" as the Temple and its altar, and the verse on lip service as a warning against habitual, heartless observance. The phrase "the LORD, who ransomed Abraham" is linked in midrash with Abraham's rescue from Nimrod's furnace (Genesis Rabbah 38:13).
views.X: The New Testament uses 29:10 for Israel's hardening (Romans 11:8), 29:13 for Jesus' critique of human traditions (Mark 7:6–7; Matthew 15:8–9), 29:14 for the cross as God's wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:19), and 29:16 with 45:9 for God's freedom as potter (Romans 9:20). The healings of 29:18 are among the signs Jesus names in Matthew 11:5.
views.F: Some futurist readers see the siege of Ariel and its sudden deliverance (29:5–8) as a preview of the final assault of the nations on Jerusalem (Zechariah 12:2–9; 14:1–5; Revelation 20:8–9), and the opening of blind eyes in 29:18 as Israel's national turning to the Messiah.

deep.h: Worship with the lips: Isaiah 29:13 in the Gospels
deep.b:
Isaiah's charge is that Judah's worship has become external: they come near with their mouths and honor God with their lips, but their hearts are far away, and their fear of God is "a command made by humans and learned by heart." The same complaint runs through the book (1:10–17; 58:1–9).

In Mark 7:6–7 and Matthew 15:8–9 Jesus quotes the verse when Pharisees and scribes criticize his disciples for eating without ritual hand-washing. His wording follows the Greek: "Their worship of me is empty; / the teachings they teach are human commands" (Mark 7:7). The Greek version had already moved the emphasis from rote fear to empty worship and human teaching, and that wording suited Jesus' point: traditions about purity can push aside the commandments of God (Mark 7:8–13). The Hebrew and the Greek agree on the core charge, that religion can become a matter of lips without the heart.

echoes: 2 Samuel 5:6–9; Ezekiel 43:15–16; 1 Samuel 28:13; Genesis 2:21; Romans 11:8; Daniel 12:4; Revelation 5:1–5; Matthew 15:8–9; Mark 7:6–7; 1 Corinthians 1:19; Jeremiah 18:1–6; Romans 9:20–21; Matthew 11:5; Amos 5:10; Matthew 6:9

settings.what: Woe to Ariel: siege and sudden rescue
settings.to: Jerusalem, called Ariel
settings.when: Probably in the years before or during Sennacherib's siege of 701 BC
settings.why: The oracle shatters the city's confidence in its festivals and its history, warning that God himself will bring it to the dust, then promises that the attackers will vanish suddenly. It teaches the hearers that both the threat and the rescue come from God.
views: Many read judgment and rescue as Isaiah's single message to Jerusalem in 701 BC.
Others think 29:5–8 was added after the city's deliverance to reinterpret the original threat.

settings.what: Blindness, the sealed scroll, and lip service
settings.by: Isaiah, and the LORD ("The Lord said," 29:13)
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and their prophets
settings.when: The same period of crisis
settings.why: The words explain why the people cannot understand what God is doing: their spiritual stupor and empty worship are themselves God's judgment. They warn that God will confound the wisdom of the wise men who lead them.

settings.what: Woe to the secret planners
settings.to: The officials planning in secret, probably the alliance with Egypt
settings.when: About 705–701 BC
settings.why: The woe tells the planners that they cannot hide from God: to plan without him is to reverse the roles of potter and clay.

settings.what: The great reversal
settings.to: The house of Jacob
settings.when: "On that day," a future soon to come ("just a very little while")
settings.why: The promise answers the chapter's darkness: the deaf will hear, the blind see, the lowly rejoice and the ruthless vanish, and Jacob will no longer be ashamed. It assures the faithful that God's purpose ends in renewal.

title: Rahab, Who Just Sits There
sum: Chapter 30 attacks Judah's alliance with Egypt. A woe falls on the "rebel children" who make plans without God and send envoys to Zoan and Hanes for Pharaoh's protection (30:1–5). An oracle follows their donkeys and camels across the dangerous Negev, loaded with treasure for a people who cannot help: Egypt is "Rahab, who just sits there" (30:6–7). Isaiah is told to write the message down as a witness, because the people want only smooth words and tell the prophets to stop seeing (30:8–11).

Their guilt is like a bulging wall about to collapse. God's offer was simple: "By turning back and resting you will be saved; in calm and in trust your strength will lie." But they refused (30:15). Yet the LORD waits to show favor. The people will weep no more, see their teacher, hear a voice saying "This is the road," throw away their idols, and enjoy rain, rich harvests and sevenfold light (30:18–26). The chapter ends with the LORD's name coming in fire to shatter Assyria while Zion sings as on Passover night, and Topheth's fire pit stands ready for the king (30:27–33).
readings: Read as a political sermon

The chapter is one of the clearest windows into Isaiah's politics: he opposed Hezekiah's alliance with Egypt against Assyria (705–701 BC), called it rebellion against God, and urged quiet trust instead. On this reading 30:15 is concrete advice: stay out of the revolt and trust the LORD.
Read as a call to faith

Others read the chapter as a call to every generation: the choice between human security (horses, alliances, smooth words) and trust in God. Verse 15 became a classic text for faith that waits quietly, and verse 18 for God's patience with those who refused.
Read as judgment and hope

The chapter moves from woe (30:1–17) to promise (30:18–26) to judgment on the enemy (30:27–33). Many scholars think the promises were added later, but the canonical order teaches that God's grace waits on the far side of judgment.

views.H: The setting is Hezekiah's revolt after Sargon II died in 705 BC, when Judah sought help from Egypt's Kushite pharaohs. In 701 BC Sennacherib defeated the Egyptian army at Eltekeh, ravaged Judah and besieged Jerusalem, which was spared (2 Kings 18–19). The fire for Assyria (30:27–33) is read as the destruction of Sennacherib's army (37:36).
views.C: Most critical scholars accept 30:1–17 as Isaiah's own words from 705–701 BC. Verses 18–26 are often seen as a later addition in the style of the book's second half, and 30:27–33 as either Isaiah's anti-Assyrian oracle or a later reworking. The writing down of the oracle (30:8) is read as evidence that Isaiah's disciples preserved his words for a later time.
views.J: Jewish tradition treats 30:15 as the classic call to teshuvah, repentance, and to quiet trust. The Talmud sets 30:26 beside 24:23 to distinguish the days of the Messiah from the world to come (Bavli Sanhedrin 91b). The "teacher" of 30:20 was read by some as God himself, who will no longer hide.
views.X: Christian readers have used 30:15 for faith and prayer ("in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength," KJV), and 30:21 for the guidance of the Spirit. The sevenfold light of 30:26 is linked with the new Jerusalem's light (Revelation 21:23), and the fire and sulfur of 30:33 with the lake of fire (Revelation 19:20; 20:10).
views.F: Futurist readers see 30:18–26 as a picture of the messianic kingdom, with Israel restored, nature renewed and light multiplied, and 30:27–33 as the destruction of the final enemy of Israel, sometimes identified with the Assyrian of the last days (Micah 5:5–6).

deep.h: Isaiah's politics: Egypt, Assyria and trust
deep.b:
After Sargon II of Assyria died in battle in 705 BC, revolts broke out across the empire. Hezekiah of Judah joined a coalition of Philistine and Phoenician cities, and his envoys sought help from Egypt, then ruled by the Kushite 25th Dynasty (30:1–7; 31:1–3). Isaiah opposed the alliance. He called it rebellion, a covenant with death (28:15), and Egypt a monster that does nothing (30:7).

Isaiah's alternative was not passivity for its own sake but trust: "By turning back and resting you will be saved" (30:15), as he had told Ahaz a generation earlier, "stay quiet. Do not be afraid" (7:4). In 701 BC Sennacherib defeated the Egyptian relief army at Eltekeh, captured, by his own count, 46 walled towns of Judah, and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage." Jerusalem survived, as Isaiah promised (37:33–35), but Judah was devastated. The chapters show a prophet who read international politics through the lens of faith.

echoes: Deuteronomy 21:18; Joshua 9:14; Deuteronomy 17:16; Psalm 87:4; Job 26:12; Habakkuk 2:2; Amos 7:12–13; Psalm 20:7; Deuteronomy 32:30; 1 Kings 22:27; Deuteronomy 5:32; Exodus 12:42; 2 Kings 23:10; Revelation 19:20; Revelation 20:10; Revelation 21:23

settings.what: Woe to the rebel children
settings.by: Isaiah, speaking for the LORD ("the LORD declares")
settings.to: Judah's leaders, who sent envoys to Egypt
settings.when: About 705–701 BC, during Hezekiah's revolt against Assyria
settings.why: The woe exposes the alliance as rebellion against God and warns that Egypt will bring only shame. It calls the leaders to consult God rather than trust a foreign power.

settings.what: The oracle about the animals of the Negev
settings.to: Judah, watching its embassy leave for Egypt
settings.when: As the caravan of tribute crossed the Negev
settings.why: The oracle mocks the costly journey through a land of terrors to buy help from a nation that will do nothing, and gives Egypt the scornful name "Rahab, who just sits there."

settings.what: The written witness and the refused offer
settings.to: "A people that defies": Judah, which silenced its prophets
settings.when: The same period; written down for a later day
settings.why: The words preserve a record that will prove God spoke in advance, and they confront the people with what they refused: salvation by returning, rest and trust. They explain the coming disaster as the result of that refusal.

settings.what: The LORD waits to show favor
settings.to: The people of Zion, in Jerusalem
settings.when: After judgment, in a future time of healing
settings.why: The promise tells a people who rejected God that God has not rejected them: he waits to show favor, will answer their cry, teach them, and heal them. It gives hope beyond the disaster announced in 30:8–17.
views: Some read it as Isaiah's promise to the faithful after 701 BC.
Many critical scholars see it as an addition from after the exile, written in the spirit of chapters 40–66.

settings.what: The LORD's fire against Assyria
settings.to: Judah, about Assyria
settings.when: Before the Assyrian army's destruction (37:36)
settings.why: The oracle promises that Assyria, which seemed unstoppable, will be destroyed by the LORD himself, and that Judah will celebrate as on Passover night. It shows that God, not Egypt, is Judah's defense.
